title: Tell the speakers that you liked their talks
author: whisper2020
tldr: Conference speaker and MC Ana Rodrigues argues that attendees should tell speakers they liked the talk. Twitter is no longer where talk feedback happens. So many speakers now get silence afterwards and wonder whether the talk landed.

keyPoints: At SmashingConf Freiburg, one attendee wanted to ask a speaker a question but felt too intimidated to approach. Rodrigues pulled the speaker into the attendee's group at the after-party.
As MC of CSS Day, Rodrigues asked each speaker at the speakers' dinner for permission to invite the audience to chat with them. Every speaker said yes.
Rodrigues joined the speaker circuit after Twitter declined. So Rodrigues never got the wave of online reactions that older speakers describe. Some of those talks drew no feedback at all.
Other speakers told Rodrigues the silence rattles them too. It is less about ego than about not knowing whether the talk went fine or flopped.
Rodrigues admits to forgetting to compliment friends who speak. Rodrigues plans to live-post and blog more from events.
Rodrigues's ask is small. A quick word or short chat is always worth it, because speakers put a lot of work in and want to know it went alright.
article.whyItMatters: The post is short and personal. Read it for the speaker's view of the after-talk silence, or to share with someone who is too shy to walk up to a speaker. The argument fits in this summary, so the original adds tone more than content.

comments.overview: A warm, agreeable thread, mostly speakers confirming that silence after a talk hurts and that one approaching stranger can change their week. The rest traded tips on making yourself easy to approach, on useful feedback, and on why remote presenting feels like talking into a void.

themes.title: Silence after a talk is hard on speakers
themes.synthesis: Speakers described days of second-guessing when nobody asks a question, and stony audiences that give no signal at all. Some blamed the setting, such as stage lighting that hides faces, or cultures where attendees treat the session as downtime. Corporate crowds may laugh at nothing, then write glowing reviews later. One commenter said a single person who came up after a panel became their co-founder.

quotes.author: lrvick
quotes.text: When zero people have any questions or feedback after, my brain tells me in a loop that nothing I said landed, and it is devastating.

quotes.author: lrvick
quotes.text: One time after a security panel at a big conference a single person came up to me after who told me what they agreed with, what they want to learn more about, and why. That person is my co-founder now.

themes.title: Specific words and questions beat "nice talk"
themes.synthesis: Several commenters said to say why you liked a talk or ask about a confusing part, since a generic compliment gives little to work with. A speaker pushed back that even a passing "nice talk" makes their day. Others said they would take hostile criticism over indifference, because it proves someone was listening. For unfriendly critics during Q&A, one tip was to visibly write down the point and thank them, which often disarms them.

quotes.author: jaffathecake
quotes.text: As someone who speaks at tech conferences, even someone just saying 'nice talk' as I walk past makes my day.

quotes.author: zitterbewegung
quotes.text: I learn more from critics than anything else and it definitely gives me evidence that people were actually understanding my talk or even where they misunderstood me.

themes.title: Speakers can make themselves easy to approach
themes.synthesis: A first-time speaker asked how to avoid sitting alone at breaks. Replies said to put "come talk to me in the hallway" on the closing slide and to stick around afterwards. Also chat with the front row before starting, and mention a topic you had no time for so people have a ready question. A side debate on jokes split between using them to pace a talk and warning that they rely on shared culture.

quotes.author: jlev1
quotes.text: mention one or two well-chosen things in your talk that are interesting and related to your topic, but that you can't go into further detail on (for lack of time). Say you'd be happy to discuss them after the talk with anyone who's interested!

quotes.author: simonw
quotes.text: "Hey, I liked your talk" is a freebie ice-breaker for anyone else, so it's much easier for them to strike up a conversation with you.

themes.title: Remote presenting is the worst case
themes.synthesis: Remote workers said presenting to a webcam with everyone's camera off gives no feedback. Emoji reactions don't fill the gap, because they pile up unevenly across presenters. One suggestion was to refuse to present unless a few people agree to respond. One commenter liked cameras-off calls because they can pace and stare at the ceiling while they talk.

quotes.author: 0xbadcafebee
quotes.text: At least in person you get the obligatory smattering of claps after the talk. When there's nothing at all, it feels like you did something wrong.

themes.title: The same goes for any creator who isn't famous
themes.synthesis: Commenters extended the advice to authors, musicians, small site owners, open source maintainers and restaurant staff, and reported long, grateful replies to fan mail. One described a TV actor who invited them to dig through the actor's garage for old tapes. The counterexample was a composer who has a copyist send stock replies, because fans don't commission the works that pay the composer.

quotes.author: rurp
quotes.text: My sense is that not many people do this and anyone who is not mega-famous rarely hears from strangers who like their work.

quotes.author: TFNA
quotes.text: I know a composer (not even that famous, just successful enough) who has his copyist answer all correspondence with stock replies, since fans don't do anything for him and just annoy him; they aren't part of the ecosystem of commissioning works that is how he gets paid.

comments.consensus: Speakers want to hear from the audience. A short compliment or question costs the attendee little and matters a lot to the speaker.
comments.dissent: A few pushed back on the premise. Some said most in-person talks aren't worth much and come from career presenters. One was brushed off by speakers busy courting people from bigger companies. And one composer reportedly finds fan mail an annoyance.

contrarian.author: jeswin
contrarian.text: While there are exceptions, there's usually very little you'd get from in-person talks. And quite often, the people who are giving these talks are serial presenters - as a lifestyle, or sometimes career building.
contrarian.why: It asks whether the talks deserve encouragement at all, a question only one reply touched, by saying the advice assumes you liked the talk.
